question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
One who eats human flesh.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Cannibal.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Cannibal" is one who eats human flesh. (नरभक्षी)
◦ Example: In the horror movie, the tribe was shown as a group of cannibals living deep in the jungle.

• The word is derived from the Spanish "Canibal", a variant of "Caribal", referring to the Carib people, who were believed by early European explorers to eat human flesh.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Scavengers (मृतभक्षी प्राणी): Animals (or people) that feed on dead or decaying flesh/waste, not necessarily human flesh (e.g., vultures, hyenas).

• Option 2: Herbivores (शाकाहारी): Animals that eat only plants and vegetation.

• Option 4: Omnivores (सर्वाहारी): Animals (or humans) that eat both plants and animal flesh.

NOTE

• Other common one-word substitutes based on eating habits: Carnivore (one who eats flesh of animals), Herbivore (one who eats only plants), Insectivore (one who eats insects), Vegetarian (one who eats only vegetables/plant food).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined part of the following sentence.
My brother always received the lion’s share of every meal that we had.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. the major portion.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom/phrase "the lion's share" means the largest or major part of something, when it is divided. (सबसे बड़ा हिस्सा)
◦ Example: The eldest son got the lion's share of his father's property.

• The phrase originates from one of Aesop's fables, in which a lion claims the largest portion of a hunted kill simply because it is the strongest and most powerful animal.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "a very small part" is the opposite meaning; it does not fit the sense of "the lion's share."

• Option 2: "the pet's share" is not an idiomatic meaning of the phrase; "lion's share" does not refer to a pet.

• Option 3: "the last bite" is incorrect; it suggests the final or smallest remaining portion, not the largest one.

NOTE

• Other idioms using animals that are frequently asked in SSC exams: "a wild goose chase" (a futile search), "crocodile tears" (fake sympathy), "let the cat out of the bag" (reveal a secret), and "take the bull by the horns" (face a difficulty boldly).

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
He and his friends / does not / want to / attend the meeting.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. does not.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject of the sentence is "He and his friends", which is a compound/plural subject (joined by "and").

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement: When two or more subjects are joined by "and", the subject becomes plural and takes a plural verb ("do/does" → "do", not "does").
◦ Example: Ram and his brothers play football daily (not "plays").

• Since the subject "He and his friends" is plural, the verb must be "do not", not "does not".
◦ Correction: He and his friends do not want to attend the meeting.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "want to" is grammatically correct; "want" correctly agrees with the plural subject once "does not" is corrected to "do not".

• Option 3: "attend the meeting" is grammatically correct; the infinitive "to attend" is properly used after "want".

• Option 4: "He and his friends" is a correctly formed compound subject; there is no error here.

NOTE

• When two subjects are joined by "as well as", "with", "along with", "in addition to", "besides", the verb agrees only with the first subject, not with the whole phrase — e.g., "The teacher, along with her students, was present."

• When two singular subjects are joined by "either...or", "neither...nor", the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined part in the following sentence.
We all have to pull our socks up for the upcoming Board exam, if we want to get outstanding grades.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. work harder than before.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "pull (one's) socks up" means to make a great effort to improve one's performance or behaviour, especially after being warned; i.e., to work harder. (कड़ी मेहनत करना/सुधार लाना)
◦ Example: After scoring poorly in the mid-terms, he decided to pull his socks up before the finals.

• Idiomatically, it evokes the image of an athlete literally pulling up loose socks before exerting greater physical effort in a race.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "act in a proper manner" describes correct behaviour/etiquette, not increased effort; it does not match the idiom.

• Option 3: "calm down impudent contempt" is unrelated to the idiom's meaning of making an effort.

• Option 4: "revive interest in old matters" describes reviving something from the past, which is not what the idiom conveys.

NOTE

• Other effort/improvement-related idioms common in SSC exams: "put one's best foot forward" (to make the best possible impression/effort), "burn the midnight oil" (to work/study late into the night), and "leave no stone unturned" (to try every possible way).

question:
The following sentence has been divided into four segments. Identify the segment in which the article has been used INCORRECTLY.
In the recent past, the IT industry has emerged / as a major contributor to an industry revenue / as well as employment / opportunity provider in the country.
option_2: In the recent past, the IT industry has emerged
option_3: as a major contributor to an industry revenue
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. as a major contributor to an industry revenue.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "an industry revenue" is grammatically incorrect. "Revenue" here is used as an uncountable/abstract noun referring to the income of the IT industry in general, so it cannot take the indefinite article "an".

• Rule — Articles with uncountable nouns: Uncountable nouns (like revenue, information, furniture, advice) are not preceded by "a/an" when used in a general sense.

• The correct expression should be "to industry revenue" or "to the industry's revenue", without the article "an".
◦ Correction: ...as a major contributor to industry revenue as well as employment...

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "opportunity provider in the country." is grammatically correct as written; no article error exists here.

• Option 2: "In the recent past, the IT industry has emerged" correctly uses the definite article "the" before "IT industry", a specific, particular industry.

• Option 4: "as well as employment" contains no article at all and is grammatically fine, since "employment" is correctly used as an uncountable noun without any article.

NOTE

• Common uncountable nouns that SSC frequently tests for article errors: information, advice, furniture, luggage, news, scenery, equipment, revenue, knowledge.

• Remember: "a/an" is used only before singular countable nouns; it is never used before plural or uncountable nouns.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Nominal
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Significant.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Nominal" means existing in name only; very small or trivial in amount (e.g., a nominal fee). (नाममात्र का/मामूली)
◦ Example: The library charges only a nominal fee for membership.

• The antonym of "Nominal" is "Significant", meaning important, substantial, or noteworthy in amount or effect. (महत्वपूर्ण/उल्लेखनीय)
◦ Example: The new policy brought about a significant change in the company's profits.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Nasty (घृणित/बुरा): Means unpleasant or unkind; it is unrelated to the size/importance sense of "nominal".

• Option 2: Sound (स्वस्थ/मजबूत): Means healthy or firmly based; it is not the opposite of "nominal".

• Option 3: Constant (स्थिर): Means unchanging or continuous; it does not oppose "nominal" in meaning.

NOTE

• "Nominal" has two related senses often tested by SSC: (i) "in name only" (e.g., a nominal head with no real power), antonym "real/actual"; and (ii) "very small" (e.g., a nominal charge), antonym "substantial/significant".

• Other confusing pairs: Trivial × Significant, Negligible × Considerable, Token × Genuine.

question: Select the sentence that does NOT have a spelling error.
option_1: There were no intermittent showers in the city, as was predicted during the whether forecast.
option_2: She is very particular about pronounciation in her classes.
option_3: The movie was very successful in the urban areas, but not among rural audiences.
option_4: There wedding was during the summer, which is why we didn’t attend it.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The movie was very successful in the urban areas, but not among rural audiences.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• All the words in Option 3 — "successful", "urban", "areas", "audiences" — are correctly spelt, so this sentence has no spelling error.

• Every other option contains one word that is commonly misspelt in competitive exams; identifying such errors requires careful attention to letters that are frequently added, dropped, or swapped.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "whether" has wrongly been used in place of "weather" — "whether" (a conjunction expressing doubt/choice) and "weather" (atmospheric conditions) are commonly confused homophones.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "pronounciation" is misspelt; the correct spelling is "pronunciation" — note there is no "o" after "pron"; it comes from "pronounce" but drops the second "o".

• Option 4 is incorrect because "There wedding" should be "Their wedding" — "there" (a place) has been wrongly used instead of the possessive pronoun "their".

NOTE

• Commonly confused homophones tested by SSC: there/their/they're, whether/weather, its/it's, affect/effect, stationary/stationery.

• Commonly misspelt words: pronunciation, occurrence, definitely, embarrass, accommodation, questionnaire.

question:
Select the option that expresses the following sentence in passive voice.
He had cleaned the bathroom.
option_1: The bathroom has cleaned by him.
option_2: The bathroom had cleaned by him.
option_3: The bathroom had been cleaned by him.
option_4: The bathroom has been cleaned by him.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The bathroom had been cleaned by him.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "He had cleaned the bathroom" is in the Past Perfect Tense.

• Rule — Past Perfect Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + had + V3 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + had been + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "the bathroom" becomes the subject; the auxiliary "had" is retained, followed by "been"; the verb "cleaned" (already V3) stays the same; and "he" becomes the agent "by him".
◦ Passive: The bathroom had been cleaned by him.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "has cleaned" is incorrect; it incorrectly uses the Present Perfect auxiliary "has" instead of the Past Perfect "had been".

• Option 2: "had cleaned by him" is incorrect because it omits "been", which is compulsory in the passive form of the Past Perfect Tense.

• Option 4: "has been cleaned" is incorrect because it wrongly uses "has been" (Present Perfect passive) instead of "had been" (Past Perfect passive).

NOTE

• The passive voice of every perfect tense always requires "been": Present Perfect Passive → has/have been + V3; Past Perfect Passive → had been + V3; Future Perfect Passive → will have been + V3.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Ashoka was the greatest than all the Mauryan Emperors .
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. of the Mauryan Emperors.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence uses the superlative degree "the greatest", but is wrongly followed by "than", which is used only with the comparative degree, not the superlative.

• Rule — Superlative Degree: When a superlative adjective (the + adjective+est / the most + adjective) is used to compare one person/thing with the rest of a group, it must be followed by "of" (for a group) or "in" (for a place/category), never by "than".
◦ Example: He is the tallest of the three brothers (not "than").

• Applying the rule: "Ashoka was the greatest than all the Mauryan Emperors" must be corrected to "Ashoka was the greatest of the Mauryan Emperors."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "all Mauryan Emperors" is incomplete and still lacks the required preposition "of"; it does not correct the error.

• Option 3: "to all another Mauryan Emperors" is grammatically faulty — "another" is a singular determiner and cannot be used with "all" or a plural noun.

• Option 4: "to other Mauryan Emperors" is incorrect because superlative comparisons require "of", not "to", and because Ashoka himself was one of the Mauryan Emperors, so "other" wrongly excludes him from the group being compared.

NOTE

• "Than" is used only with the comparative degree (e.g., "greater than", "better than"); it is never used with the superlative degree.

• Common superlative structures: "the best of all", "the largest in the world", "one of the best players".

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Concede
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Deny.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Concede" means to admit that something is true, or to yield/grant something reluctantly. (स्वीकार करना/मान लेना)
◦ Example: After the results were declared, the losing candidate conceded defeat.

• The antonym of "Concede" is "Deny", meaning to state that something is not true; to refuse to admit or grant. (इनकार करना)
◦ Example: He denied any involvement in the scandal.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Surrender (आत्मसमर्पण करना): Means to give up or yield completely, which is close in meaning to "concede", not its opposite.

• Option 2: Battle (संघर्ष करना): Means to fight or struggle; it is not directly opposite to "concede" in meaning.

• Option 3: Avow (खुले तौर पर स्वीकार करना): Means to openly admit or declare, which is a synonym of "concede", not an antonym.

NOTE

• Related word pairs often tested: Concede × Refute/Deny, Admit × Dispute, Acknowledge × Contest.

• "Concede" is also used in the context of games/elections to mean "to accept defeat", e.g., "The team conceded the match in the final minute.".

question:
Identify the INCORRECTLY spelt word in the following sentence.
Parul is known as a rigteous and honest lady.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. rigteous.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "rigteous" is misspelt in the sentence; the correct spelling is "righteous", meaning morally right or virtuous. (धर्मी/नेक)
◦ Example: Parul is known as a righteous and honest lady.

• Spelling key: RIGHT + EOUS. Note the silent "gh" after "ri" — it comes from the root word "right", and the missing "h" is the common error in this word.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "known" is correctly spelt; it is the past participle of "know".

• Option 3: "lady" is correctly spelt; there is no error here.

• Option 4: "honest" is correctly spelt.

NOTE

• Other words derived from "right" that are frequently misspelt: rightful, righteousness, upright.

• Words with a silent "gh" that SSC often tests: though, thorough, daughter, night, sight, weight.

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
P- for a
Q- exercise daily
R- one must
S- good body
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. RQPS.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given parts are: P- for a, Q- exercise daily, R- one must, S- good body.

• Reading the parts together in the order R-Q-P-S gives a grammatically complete and meaningful sentence: "One must exercise daily for a good body."

• R (one must) naturally begins the sentence as the subject + modal verb; Q (exercise daily) follows as the main verb phrase; P (for a) introduces the purpose/reason; and S (good body) completes the phrase begun by "for a".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "PRQS" is incorrect; it produces the meaningless order "for a / one must / exercise daily / good body".

• Option 2: "PRSQ" is incorrect; it produces "for a / one must / good body / exercise daily", which is grammatically broken.

• Option 4: "PQRS" is incorrect; it produces "for a / exercise daily / one must / good body", which does not form a coherent sentence.

NOTE

• In parajumble questions, first identify the part containing the subject and main verb (usually the starting point), then look for connecting words/phrases ("for", "and", "but") that link the remaining parts logically.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Bombastic
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Simple.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Bombastic" means (of language) high-sounding but with little meaning; pompous or inflated in style. (आडंबरपूर्ण/अलंकृत)
◦ Example: The politician's bombastic speech impressed no one, as it lacked any real substance.

• The antonym of "Bombastic" is "Simple", meaning plain, easy to understand, without unnecessary embellishment. (सरल)
◦ Example: She explained the concept in simple, clear language.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Wicked (दुष्ट): Means evil or morally wrong; unrelated to the "pompous language" sense of "bombastic".

• Option 3: Elevated (उच्च): Means raised or lofty in style, which is actually close in meaning to "bombastic", not its opposite.

• Option 4: Pastoral (ग्रामीण): Relates to rural or country life; it has no direct connection to "bombastic".

NOTE

• Words similar in meaning to "bombastic": grandiloquent, pompous, pretentious, flowery, verbose.

• Antonym pairs on the same theme frequently tested by SSC: Bombastic × Simple/Plain, Verbose × Concise, Ornate × Austere.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Forgive
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Loathe.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Forgive" means to stop feeling angry or resentful towards someone for an offence; to pardon. (क्षमा करना)
◦ Example: She forgave her friend for the misunderstanding.

• The antonym of "Forgive" is "Loathe", meaning to feel intense dislike or disgust for someone or something. (घृणा करना)
◦ Example: He loathed the idea of working with dishonest people.

• While "forgive" reflects letting go of negative feelings towards someone, "loathe" reflects holding onto and intensifying negative feelings — making the two words opposite in emotional direction.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Unburden (बोझ हल्का करना): Means to relieve oneself of a load or worry (e.g., to unburden one's mind); it is not opposite in meaning to "forgive".

• Option 2: Requite (बदला चुकाना/प्रतिफल देना): Means to make a return for a favour or service; though it can occasionally carry the sense of repaying an injury, its primary modern sense is to reciprocate, not to oppose forgiveness directly.

• Option 3: Clear (निर्दोष सिद्ध करना): Means to declare someone free from blame or guilt, which is close in meaning to "forgive"/"pardon", not its opposite.

NOTE

• Related antonym pairs frequently tested: Pardon × Punish, Absolve × Condemn, Excuse × Blame.

• "Forgive" is often used with the prepositions "forgive someone for something", e.g., "I forgive you for being late.".

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the word in brackets to fill in the blank.
He said that he lacks the ___________ to stand in a queue. (patience)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. endurance.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Patience" means the capacity to accept or tolerate delay, trouble, or suffering without getting upset. (धैर्य/सहनशीलता)

• "Endurance" is the closest synonym among the given options, meaning the ability to bear or withstand hardship, difficulty, or delay without complaint. (सहनशक्ति)
◦ Example: He said that he lacks the endurance to stand in a queue.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "relevance" means being closely connected or appropriate to the matter at hand; it has no relation to "patience".

• Option 2: "elegance" means refined grace or stylishness; it is unrelated to the meaning of "patience".

• Option 4: "acceptance" means the act of agreeing to or receiving something; while related to tolerating a situation, it does not specifically convey the sense of enduring delay/hardship the way "endurance" does.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "patience" useful for SSC: perseverance, tolerance, fortitude, forbearance, composure.

• "Endurance" is also commonly used in the context of physical stamina, e.g., "an endurance test/race".

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
(a) the Industrial Revolution denotes
(b) and continued until the middle of the 19th century
(c) a significant period of social, economic and technological revolution
(d) that commenced in the latter part of the 18th century
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. acdb.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given parts are: (a) the Industrial Revolution denotes, (b) and continued until the middle of the 19th century, (c) a significant period of social, economic and technological revolution, (d) that commenced in the latter part of the 18th century.

• Reading the parts in the order a-c-d-b forms a grammatically correct and logically sequenced sentence: "The Industrial Revolution denotes a significant period of social, economic and technological revolution that commenced in the latter part of the 18th century and continued until the middle of the 19th century."

• (a) introduces the subject and verb ("the Industrial Revolution denotes"); (c) completes the object ("a significant period..."); (d) adds a relative clause describing when it began; and (b), joined by "and", adds when it ended — following logically after "commenced" with "continued".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "dcba" is incorrect; starting with "(d) that commenced..." leaves the relative pronoun "that" without an antecedent, making the sentence ungrammatical.

• Option 3: "abcd" is incorrect; it produces "the Industrial Revolution denotes / and continued until the middle of the 19th century / a significant period...", which is not logically sequenced.

• Option 4: "cadb" is incorrect; starting with "(c) a significant period..." leaves the sentence without its main subject-verb opening.

NOTE

• In parajumble questions with relative clauses ("that/which/who"), always ensure the clause is placed immediately after the noun it describes, and that connectors like "and" join two similar/parallel ideas (here, two verb phrases — "commenced" and "continued").

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
The ship launched out on a journey by water or sea of discovery.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. voyage.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "voyage" means a long journey involving travel by sea or in space. (समुद्री यात्रा)
◦ Example: The sailors set out on a voyage across the Atlantic Ocean.

• The underlined phrase "journey by water or sea" is best and most concisely replaced by the single word "voyage", which carries exactly this meaning.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "rendezvous" (मिलन-स्थल): Means a meeting at an agreed time and place; it has nothing to do with travel by sea.

• Option 3: "verso": A printing/publishing term referring to the left-hand page of an open book; it is completely unrelated in meaning.

• Option 4: "vespers": Refers to evening prayers or a religious evening service; it has no connection to travel by sea.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutes for types of journeys often tested by SSC: "expedition" (a journey for a specific purpose, e.g. exploration), "pilgrimage" (a journey to a sacred place), "odyssey" (a long, eventful journey), and "trek" (a long, arduous journey, especially on foot).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the word in the brackets to fill in the blank.
The pool was too ______ at this end for kids to play. [SHALLOW]
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. deep.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Shallow" means having little depth; not deep. (उथला)

• The antonym of "Shallow" is "Deep", meaning extending far down from the top or surface. (गहरा)
◦ Example: The pool was too deep at this end for kids to play.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "green" refers to a colour; it is unrelated to the depth of the pool.

• Option 2: "blue" also refers to a colour, and does not describe depth.

• Option 4: "cold" describes temperature, not depth; it does not fit as the antonym of "shallow".

NOTE

• "Shallow" also has a figurative sense meaning superficial or lacking depth of character/thought (e.g., "a shallow person"), whose antonym in that sense is "profound" or "deep" as well.

• Other depth-related antonym pairs: Deep × Shallow, Profound × Superficial, Thorough × Cursory.

question:
Select the option that can substitute/replace the bracketed word correctly and complete the sentence.
I said I (don’t) understand.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. didn't.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence begins with "I said...", which is in the Past Tense, i.e., it is indirect/reported speech introduced by a past reporting verb.

• Rule — Backshift of Tense in Reported Speech: When the reporting verb is in the past tense, the tense of the reported clause also shifts backward; the Simple Present ("don't") changes to the Simple Past ("didn't").
◦ Direct: He said, "I don't understand." → Indirect: He said (that) he didn't understand.

• Applying the rule: "I said I (don't) understand" must be corrected to "I said I didn't understand."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "doesn't" is incorrect; it is still in the present tense and does not agree with the first-person subject "I" either ("doesn't" is used with he/she/it).

• Option 2: "am doing" is incorrect; it wrongly uses the present continuous tense, which is not the correct backshift of "don't understand" (a state verb not normally used in continuous form).

• Option 4: "done" is incorrect; it is a past participle form and cannot stand alone as the main verb here.

NOTE

• Common tense backshifts in reported speech: am/is/are → was/were; do/does → did; have/has → had; will → would; can → could.

• Note that "understand" is a stative verb and is generally not used in the continuous form (e.g., not "is understanding").

question:
Select the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
Why didn’t she bring her son to my house?
option_1: Why wasn’t her son brought by her to my house?
option_2: Why isn’t her son brought to my house?
option_3: Why wasn’t her son brought to my house?
option_4: Why isn’t her son brought by you to my house?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Why wasn't her son brought by her to my house?

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "Why didn't she bring her son to my house?" is a negative interrogative sentence in the Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Passive of Negative Interrogative (Simple Past):
◦ Active: Wh-word + didn't + Subject + V1 + Object?
◦ Passive: Wh-word + wasn't/weren't + Object(as new subject) + V3 + by + Subject?

• Applying the rule: the object "her son" becomes the subject; the auxiliary "didn't" changes to "wasn't" (singular); the verb "bring" becomes the past participle "brought"; and "she" becomes the agent, retained as "by her" since the doer must still be specified.
◦ Passive: Why wasn't her son brought by her to my house?

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Why isn't her son brought to my house?" is incorrect because it wrongly uses the present tense auxiliary "isn't" instead of the past tense "wasn't", and also drops the agent "by her".

• Option 3: "Why wasn't her son brought to my house?" is incorrect because it drops the agent "by her"; since the original sentence specifically names "she" as the subject, the passive must retain "by her" to preserve the meaning.

• Option 4: "Why isn't her son brought by you to my house?" is incorrect because it wrongly uses the present tense "isn't" and also wrongly changes the agent from "her" to "you", altering the meaning of the sentence.

NOTE

• In passive voice, the agent ("by + doer") may only be dropped when the doer is unknown, unimportant, or obvious from context — never when the active sentence explicitly names a specific subject.

We naturally seek the company of those whose (1) _________ are the same as our own. Fools do not like the (2) _________ of wise men, and wise men avoid fools. solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. tastes.

• The sentence reads: "We naturally seek the company of those whose (1) _________ are the same as our own." This requires a word describing personal likes, preferences, or inclinations shared between people, which fits naturally with "the company of those whose ___ are the same as our own."

• "Tastes" (plural) refers to a person's preferences or liking for particular things (e.g., music, food, style), which fits perfectly, as people naturally gravitate toward others who share similar likes and preferences.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "organisations" does not fit; the sentence is about personal compatibility with people, not about shared organisational membership.

• Option 2: "institutes" is incorrect for the same reason; it refers to institutions, not personal likes/preferences.

• Option 3: "apathy" means a lack of interest or concern; it does not make sense to say two people's "apathy are the same", and most people would not describe shared indifference as a reason for seeking company.

NOTE

• The passage is built around the well-known idea/proverb "A man is known by the company he keeps", i.e., people tend to associate with others who share similar tastes, values, and character.

• Option 3: "grave" means serious or solemn in manner, which is also similar to "serious-minded", not its opposite.

• "Frivolous" is a commonly tested SSC vocabulary word meaning silly, trivial, or lacking seriousness — its synonyms include flippant, superficial, silly, and its antonyms include serious, solemn, earnest.
